```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# cograph is a suggested package; its flow and transition chunks are skipped
# when it is not installed, so the vignette still builds.
has_cograph <- requireNamespace("cograph", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  echo = TRUE,
  fig.width = 7.5,
  fig.height = 6,
  dpi = 120,
  message = TRUE,
  warning = TRUE
)
options(digits = 2)
```

This is a visual gallery of every VaSSTra plot, run on the longitudinal
engagement data from
[Chapter 11 of *Learning Analytics Methods and Tutorials*](https://lamethods.org/book1/chapters/ch11-vasstra/ch11-vasstra.html).
It follows the method's own order: the state views, the sequence views, the
trajectory views, and the combined per-trajectory grid (all base graphics,
no `ggplot2` dependency), then the `evaluate()` selection panels, and last
the `cograph`-rendered flow and transition networks. Every view shares one
state palette and one state order, both of which can be pinned on the fit
with `state_colors` and `state_order`.

It focuses only on the plots. For the workflow around them (running
`vasstra()`, comparing counts, reading fit indices, relabeling groups, and
extracting tidy tables), see `vignette("get-started")` and
`vignette("vasstra-tutorial")`, and `vignette("clustering-algorithms")` for
the estimation methods.

## The fit

Every figure below is drawn from one fit, and to keep the gallery about the
plots rather than the tuning, that fit is the fully automatic default:
`vasstra(engagement)` detects the roles, selects the number of states and
trajectories, and fits them. It settles on five states and three
trajectories here, drawn in their discovery order on the default palette.
Naming, reordering, and recolouring are shown in *Palette and state order*
below; they change how a plot reads, not which plot each call draws.

```{r fit}
library(VaSSTra)
data("engagement", package = "VaSSTra")

fit <- vasstra(engagement)
```

## State overview: profile + bars + heatmap + sizes

`type = "all"` draws the four state views together on the shared palette;
the profile heatmap reads with the first state as its top row, matching the
bars, sizes, and legends.

```{r state-all, fig.height = 8}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "all")
```

Each view is also available alone:

```{r state-profile}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "profile")
```

```{r state-bars}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "bars")
```

```{r state-heatmap}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "heatmap")
```

```{r state-sizes}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "sizes")
```

## Indicators by state

`type = "variables"` takes the profile apart along time. It draws one panel
per time point and, within each, a grouped boxplot of every clustering
indicator split by state, so the aggregated profile above becomes a question
you can check at each moment: does each indicator keep separating the states
throughout, or only on average? The indicators stay on the scale the states
were clustered on, so the shared y-axis is comparable across panels, and the
call returns the tidy time-by-variable-by-state medians behind the boxes.

```{r state-variables, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 9}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "variables")
```

`by_time = FALSE` pools the time points into a single panel, the boxplot
counterpart of the profile plot: one box per indicator and state, over all
observations.

```{r state-variables-pooled, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(fit, which = "states", type = "variables", by_time = FALSE)
```

`state_descriptives()` is the numeric companion: one row per state and
indicator with the count, mean, standard deviation, median, and range.
`scale = "original"` reports the raw indicators instead of the clustered
(standardized) ones.

```{r state-descriptives}
head(state_descriptives(fit))
```

`by_time = TRUE` matches the faceted plot: it adds a `time` column and
reports the same statistics per state, indicator, and time point.

```{r state-descriptives-by-time}
head(state_descriptives(fit, by_time = TRUE))
```

## Palette and state order

Two arguments control how states display everywhere. `state_colors` pins a
palette on the fit (a named vector is matched by state and survives
reordering and `set_labels()`), and `state_order` fixes the order the states
read in every plot (stacking, legends, transition and flow nodes),
independent of the order the clusters were discovered in. Both are stored on
the fit and reused by every plot, so the styling is set once; a `colors`
argument on an individual `plot()` call overrides them for that call alone.

```{r palette-stored, fig.height = 5.5}
fit_styled <- vasstra(
  engagement,
  state_labels = c("Disengaged", "Average", "Active"),
  state_order  = c("Active", "Average", "Disengaged"),
  state_colors = c(Disengaged = "#D55E00", Average = "#0072B2", Active = "#009E73")
)
plot(fit_styled, type = "distribution")
```

## All sequences: heatmap (default), distribution, index

Every plot containing state sequences is rendered by
`Nestimate::sequence_plot()`. The heatmap is the default view for the
complete sequence set.

```{r sequences-heatmap}
plot(fit, which = "sequences")
```

```{r sequences-distribution}
plot(fit, which = "sequences", type = "distribution")
```

```{r sequences-index}
plot(fit, which = "sequences", type = "index")
```

## Trajectories: distribution, index, heatmap

```{r trajectories-distribution}
plot(fit, type = "distribution")
```

```{r trajectories-index}
plot(fit, type = "index")
```

```{r trajectories-heatmap}
plot(fit, type = "heatmap")
```

## The combined per-trajectory grid

Passing several views in `type` composes them into one figure with **one
row per trajectory and one column per view**, in the order requested. This
is the standard per-cluster VaSSTra display, drawn in one call with a shared
ordered legend. The transition column needs the suggested `cograph`
package.

```{r trajectories-grid, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 8, eval = has_cograph}
plot(fit, type = c("index", "distribution", "transition"))
```

## Evaluation panels

`plot(evaluate(fit))` draws the selection curve, per-cluster silhouette
widths, and group sizes for both clustering steps. The state and trajectory
rows use distinct palettes, so the two groupings are not read as
corresponding.

```{r evaluation, fig.height = 7}
plot(evaluate(fit))
```

## Choice comparisons across methods

The explicit comparison draws a metric-aware plot, on the shared palette
with light gridlines.

```{r state-choices}
state_options <- state_choices(
  engagement,
  n_states = 2:5,
  method = c("kmeans", "pam", "ward.D2", "lpa"),
  lpa_model = "EEI",
  seed = 22294
)
plot(state_options, metric = "silhouette")
plot(state_options, metric = "bic", groups = "lpa/EEI")
```

## Flow plots (cograph)

`flow_plot()` renders state movement between consecutive time points
through cograph, on the same palette and state order as every other plot,
and returns a `ggplot` object rather than drawing base graphics. Aggregated
bands and individual lines are the two views:

```{r flow-alluvial, eval = has_cograph}
flow_plot(fit)
```

```{r flow-individual, eval = has_cograph}
flow_plot(fit, type = "individual")
```

The `vignette("flow-plots")` article covers the rest: colouring by
destination or by first/last state, restricting to one trajectory,
line bundling, thresholding negligible flows, and tuning a figure for a
manuscript.

## Transition network (Nestimate builds, cograph draws)

Node size is a transition-network centrality from
`Nestimate::net_centrality()`; the network comes from
`Nestimate::build_tna()`. Drawn by `cograph::splot()`; returns the
tidy node table invisibly. The paired form places the sequences beside the
network on one shared palette.

```{r transition-default, fig.height = 6, eval = has_cograph}
transition_plot(fit)
```

```{r transition-paired, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4.6, eval = has_cograph}
transition_plot(fit, sequences = TRUE)
```

The centralities are also available as a tidy table:

```{r transition-centrality}
transition_centrality(fit)
```

See `vignette("flow-plots")` for the centrality-driven node sizing
(`size`, `weights`, `loops`), the per-trajectory networks, and the other
paired views.
